entry.title: Building GeoNLI: Refine, Generate, Filter, Reason

link.title: Building GeoNLI: Refine, Generate, Filter, Reason

entry.content:
For Inter-IIT Tech Meet 14.0, the ISRO problem statement asked for a natural-language interface to Earth-observation (EO) imagery. Our team (Team 58: Karan Gandhi, Laksh Jain, Romit Mohane, Shreyans Jain, Umang Shikarvar and Viraj Vekaria) ended up with a Silver Medal. This post walks through how the system was put together and, more usefully, why each piece is there. The short version of the project is on the project page; code is at Umang-Shikarvar/GeoNLI.

The problem in one picture

One interface, three tasks: write a caption for a scene, answer a question (yes/no, a number, or a free-form answer), and ground a referring expression such as “the smallest plane near the vehicle” with a box on the image. Inputs can be RGB, false-colour composite (FCC) or SAR.

Two properties of EO data shaped everything. First, objects are small and crowded, so coordinate-token grounding by a VLM tends to merge neighbours and returns axis-aligned boxes for objects that are anything but axis-aligned. Second, the inputs are spectrally strange: a vision encoder trained on RGB reads red vegetation in an FCC image as something very different from vegetation.

Decision 1: fix the input before touching the model

Rather than hope the VLM generalises across modalities, we add a deterministic domain-adaptation layer. For FCC images (channels map to NIR, Red, Green) we synthesise the missing blue channel with a linear model from the literature (Patra et al.):

\[B_{synth} = a_B + b_B \cdot G + c_B \cdot R + d_B \cdot \mathrm{NIR}\]

with coefficients \(a_B = 13.9053\), \(b_B = 0.8733\), \(c_B = -0.1382\), \(d_B = -0.1006\), then restack as natural colour. For SAR we use a Pix2Pix SAR-to-RGB generator, which keeps geometry while inventing plausible colour. Real-ESRGAN follows as a 4x sharpener only, so the downstream segmenter sees crisp edges and not GAN blur.

The risk, which we wrote down in the report, is that the generator can hallucinate or erase detail, and fixed FCC coefficients assume standard band responses. We accepted that trade because everything downstream got simpler.

Decision 2: segmentation-first grounding

We did not ask a VLM to emit coordinates. The grounding pipeline has four stages, which gave the report its name.

Refine. Mistral-7B strips spatial language from the query (“leftmost airplane” becomes “airplane”), since a segmentation model has no idea what “leftmost” means.

Generate. SAM3, fine-tuned on VRSBench, produces dense masks. We recover oriented bounding boxes from the contours with rotating calipers, which is why a model supervised on axis-aligned boxes can still output rotated ones.

Filter. SAM3 happily segments shadows, gangways and service vehicles. We crop each candidate, rotate it upright, and score it with CLIP against the class text; anything under 0.25 is dropped, then NMS removes duplicates.

Reason. The surviving boxes are drawn on the image with index, colour and area, and Qwen3-VL picks the indices matching the full query, returning JSON with a rationale. Selecting an index is a much easier task for a VLM than regressing coordinates.

Fine-tuning SAM3 on sparse labels

VRSBench does not label every instance (five of fifty cars might be annotated). A detector trained to find all instances is penalised for correct detections. So we trained SAM3 to segment the specific instance referenced by the query, with a composite loss:

\[L_{total} = \lambda_{ce} L_{ce} + \lambda_{pres} L_{pres} + \lambda_{box} L_{box} + \lambda_{giou} L_{giou}\]

A focal classification term, a presence term (so the model can say “nothing here”), an L1 box term and a GIoU term. What mattered in practice:

  • Aggressive loss weights were unstable; we lowered the classification and presence weights from 20 to 10 and the focal positive weight from 10 to 5.
  • One epoch was best. More epochs overfit the prompt phrasing and hurt zero-shot behaviour.
  • We froze the ViT and text encoder and trained only the prompt encoder and mask decoder; fine-tuning the whole model diverged after two epochs.
  • Gradient clipping, mixed precision and warmup kept training stable.

Decision 3: captions that must agree with detections

Free-form VLM captions invent objects. Our captioning is grounding-first: we run the grounding pipeline, serialise the verified detections (class, box, confidence) into the prompt as hints, and instruct the model to use only those. Qwen3-VL was fine-tuned on VRSBench captions with LoRA and bf16 on a single A100 for fast iteration. The ablation showed hinted generation raises object-level precision. We also learned that super-resolution on low-GSD crops helps attribute recognition (roof colour, vehicle type) but sometimes adds artefacts, so we use it selectively.

The cost is a recall bottleneck: if SAM3 misses an object, the caption cannot mention it.

Decision 4: do not let the VLM do arithmetic

VLMs miscount dense clusters and cannot compute area or perimeter. The VQA system therefore has a router (Mistral-7B) with three outcomes:

  • Semantic questions go straight to a fine-tuned Qwen3-VL-8B.
  • Binary questions run the grounding pipeline, and the VLM answers over the filtered objects.
  • Numeric questions (count, length, area, perimeter) run grounding and then a deterministic geometry engine computes the number.

If the OBB pipeline fails to parse or is ambiguous, the system falls back to the fine-tuned VLM so an answer is always returned. The VLM alone scored 90.86 binary accuracy but only 0.56 on the numeric score (MAE 0.73, RMSE 1.41), which is exactly the gap the geometry engine targets.

What the numbers said

On the VRSBench validation split, strict grounding accuracy (Acc@0.7) was 31.3% against 19.9% for GeoChat and 13.6% for LLaVA-1.5, and on the non-unique (crowded) subset it was 32.5% against 18.0% for GeoChat. At the loose threshold (Acc@0.5) GeoChat is still ahead on the unique subset (57.4 vs 52.5), so the win is about precision and clutter, not everywhere. Captioning reached BLEU-1 52.9 and BERTScore F1 0.897; our BLEU-4 (12.6) is a little below LLaVA-1.5 because our captions are terse. Removing the CLIP filter cost about 12% IoU.

Shipping it

The system is a Flask backend with a model manager that wraps each pipeline behind adapters, a single POST /geoNLI/eval endpoint with an evaluation mode and an interactive mode, a React/Vite dashboard, and a Vercel proxy in front. All models are open-source and run locally on GPUs.

What I would do differently

  • Errors cascade. A hierarchical pipeline is explainable but its recall ceiling is set by the first stage.
  • The router is a single point of fragility, and malformed VLM JSON can slip past even regex extraction and repair.
  • Rotating calipers assumes convex shapes, so U-shaped buildings get loose boxes.
  • A learned way to threshold the CLIP filter would beat a fixed 0.25.

The biggest lesson was to put deterministic code wherever a precise answer exists and keep the generative models for the parts that really need language. That separation is also what made the system debuggable under competition time pressure.

Full details: GeoNLI project page and the code.
entry.summary: How our Inter-IIT 14.0 ISRO solution handles captioning, VQA and oriented grounding on satellite imagery, and why we split perception from logic.

entry.title: Closing the Early-Stage Blind Spot in Histotripsy Monitoring with Dice-Focal Loss

link.title: Closing the Early-Stage Blind Spot in Histotripsy Monitoring with Dice-Focal Loss

entry.content:
Histotripsy is one of the more striking ideas in therapeutic ultrasound. Instead of heating tissue, it fires microsecond pulses with very high peak negative pressure into a target and creates a cloud of cavitation bubbles that mechanically liquefies it. No heat, no ionizing radiation, and no heat-sink problem near blood vessels. The catch is that you need to know what you have destroyed. This post is about the part of that problem I worked on at the MUSE Lab (IIT Gandhinagar): segmenting the ablation zone from B-mode ultrasound, and in particular, why our models first failed exactly when the clinician cares most.

The problem: you cannot see the lesion

Histotripsy systems are usually paired with B-mode imaging for targeting. But the lesion’s appearance changes over the treatment. Early on, the bubble cloud shows up as a hyperechoic region; later, once tissue is fragmented, it becomes hypoechoic. In between, contrast is low and the region is speckled. Right now, confirming that an ablation worked often means going to CT or MRI, which adds time, cost and complexity. A model that outlines the ablated region directly on the live ultrasound image could close that loop.

A previous paper from our collaborators (Miao et al., IEEE TBME 2024) trained a ResNet-18 with transfer learning to do this. It worked reasonably overall, but it had a blind spot: the Dice similarity coefficient was below 20% for fewer than 500 applied pulses. The early frames are precisely when you would want to adjust a treatment, so this was the gap we wanted to close.

Setting up a fair comparison

I wanted every number in our study to be comparable to the earlier work, so we used the same experimental data. The data come from agarose phantoms containing a red-blood-cell layer. When histotripsy ablates the layer, it changes color, so a synchronized camera records ground truth while the ultrasound probe records B-mode images. Otsu-thresholding the optical images and co-registering them with fiducial markers gives masks in ultrasound coordinates.

The dataset is small: nine experimental runs, 880 ultrasound images (an image every 20 pulses). One run is held out for validation, and four fully independent phantoms (400 images) are used only for testing. That is the same test set as the prior paper. Small data has a real consequence: you need to be careful with leakage, so we used a leave-one-dataset-out strategy and dropped a few timestamps to avoid overlap.

Before changing anything, I re-implemented the ResNet-18 baseline in PyTorch. Its global accuracy (0.954 vs 0.956) and weighted IoU (0.916 vs 0.916) landed very close to the published numbers, which gave me confidence that later gains were not an artifact of a different pipeline.

What we tried

We evaluated six architectures spanning 3.2M to 58.6M parameters:

  • ResNet-18 (the baseline, adapted to segmentation)
  • MobileNetV3 LR-ASPP
  • SegFormer-B0
  • MobileViT-v2 with a U-Net decoder
  • EfficientNet-B0 U-Net
  • DeepLabV3 with a ResNet-101 backbone, as a high-capacity reference

All were fine-tuned from public pretrained weights and trained with identical settings (AdamW, learning rate \(10^{-3}\), cosine annealing with warm restarts, batch size 16, 128x512 input) so architecture was the only variable.

The more important variable turned out to be the loss.

Why Dice alone struggles here

In early frames, ablated pixels are a minuscule fraction of the image. Cross-entropy is swamped by background. Dice loss helps with imbalance, but when the foreground is a few faint pixels its gradients are noisy, and the model can score decently by predicting almost nothing. We added a focal term:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Focal}}(p_t) = -\alpha_t (1-p_t)^{\gamma} \log(p_t), \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{Total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{Dice}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{Focal}}\]

with \(\alpha = 1\) and \(\gamma = 2\). The \((1-p_t)^\gamma\) factor shrinks the loss on pixels the model already classifies confidently, which in this problem is nearly all of the background. What is left is the hard, sparse foreground. Both terms are weighted 1.0.

What worked

The loss change was the single most consistent improvement. For every architecture we tested, Dice-Focal beat Dice alone: ResNet-18 went from DSC 0.757 to 0.791, and EfficientNet-B0 from 0.748 to 0.831.

On the 400 independent test images, the headline comparison is:

Method Global Acc. Mean IoU Weighted IoU
Prior ResNet-18 0.956 0.765 0.916
EfficientNet-B0 + Dice-Focal 0.968 0.838 0.939
DeepLabV3 + Dice-Focal 0.960 0.812 0.927

The pulse-dependence curve is the one I care about most. With the prior training setup, the baseline sits near zero below 500 pulses. Both EfficientNet-B0 and DeepLabV3 with Dice-Focal loss rise steeply from around 300 pulses and plateau at about 0.83 and 0.88 respectively, versus 0.63 for the baseline.

The area plot shows a second, quieter failure of the baseline: it over-predicts the ablated area throughout treatment, around 130 mm\(^2\) even when the true ablation is zero (Pearson r = 0.61, MAE 49.8 mm\(^2\)). EfficientNet-B0 tracks the true area from the outset (r = 0.967, MAE 5.98 mm\(^2\)), and DeepLabV3 is tightest (r = 0.978, MAE 5.03 mm\(^2\)). For a clinician, an area estimate that is right is more useful than a pretty mask.

The small model wins

The pleasant surprise was efficiency. EfficientNet-B0 U-Net has 7.9M parameters, 7.4 times fewer than DeepLabV3 (58.6M), and still had the better Dice (0.831 vs 0.802) and mean IoU. It runs at roughly 13.5 ms per image on an A100. DeepLabV3’s strength is the area-tracking correlation, which we attribute to its multi-scale atrous convolutions. As a reference upper bound it is useful; as a deployable model, the small U-Net makes more sense.

What did not work, or is not solved

  • Bigger was not better. The 58.6M-parameter DeepLabV3 did not beat EfficientNet-B0 on Dice, and the lightweight options (MobileNetV3, MobileViT-v2) did not either.
  • Dice-only EfficientNet-B0 was unstable. Its DSC looked moderate at 0.748, but its area correlation was negative (r = -0.668). That is a good reminder that a single overlap metric can hide a model that is not tracking the physical quantity you care about.
  • Under about 100 pulses is still hard. The class imbalance there is extreme and we did not solve it. Targeted augmentation is the next thing I would try.
  • Phantoms are not tissue. Everything is in-vitro agarose. Ex-vivo and in-vivo data will change speckle statistics and annotation quality; semi-supervised or domain-adaptation methods may reduce the labeling burden.
  • Labels are noisy. Ground truth comes from thresholded optical images, and annotation variability was a recurring challenge noted in the project.

Takeaways

  1. When the signal you care about is a sparse minority of pixels, change the loss before you change the architecture. Of all the changes we made, this was the most consistent.
  2. Re-implement the baseline and match the published numbers first. It is tedious, but it is what makes the comparison credible.
  3. Track the physical quantity (here, lesion area) and not only an overlap score.
  4. A 7.9M-parameter model that matches or beats a 58.6M one is the more interesting result for a system that has to run beside a therapy device.

Links

  • Project page: Histotripsy bubble-cloud segmentation
  • Code: ShreyansJain04/BubbleSegmentation
entry.summary: How a loss-function change, more than a bigger network, fixed segmentation of sparse bubble clouds in B-mode ultrasound.

entry.title: Detecting AI-Generated Images at 32x32: Our Adobe Challenge at Inter-IIT 13.0

link.title: Detecting AI-Generated Images at 32x32: Our Adobe Challenge at Inter-IIT 13.0

entry.content:
Inter-IIT Tech Meet 13.0 at IIT Bombay included a computer-vision problem statement from Adobe Research on detecting AI-generated images and explaining the decision. Our team (Team 64) earned a Silver Medal. This is the story of how the detector came together. The summary lives on the project page and the code at the repository.

The two tasks

  1. Detection. Classify images from a dataset of 32x32 pixels as real or AI-generated. Fakes came from various GANs, diffusion models and Adobe Firefly. CIFAKE was provided, with a ResNet50 baseline in the problem statement.
  2. Explanation. For images flagged as fake, identify artifacts and give a short description.

The 32x32 resolution is a double-edged sword. It makes models small and cheap, but it blurs exactly the details (textures, lighting, boundaries) that you would normally use to spot a fake.

Picking the architecture

We first benchmarked families on CIFAKE (60,000 images, 50,000 train and 10,000 test): LeViT, a hybrid of convolutions and transformer attention designed for fast inference, and EfficientNet, a compound-scaled CNN. We also plotted parameters against inference time to keep the model practical.

Plain LeViT-192 scored 95.87%, below LeViT-128 (97.14%) and EfficientNet-b0 (98.47%). The model was not the whole story, so the next gains had to come from features and data.

Neighboring Pixel Relationships

Generators build images through up-sampling operators, which leave local correlations between neighbouring pixels. Neighboring Pixel Relationships (NPR) represent exactly that. They work in the spatial domain, as opposed to frequency-based detectors, and the NPR paper reports generalisation across 28 generator models with an 11.6% margin over earlier methods. Feeding NPR features to the classifier was the single most useful change: LeViT-128 + NPR reached 98.88%.

Training recipe

Two stages. First, pretrain LeViT-192 to separate real from fake on 4 million images subsampled from GenImage, resized to 32x32 and spanning ImageNet-1K classes across generators. Second, fine-tune on CIFAKE, whose classes match CIFAR-10, which is what the final evaluation used.

Robustness mattered because real images get compressed, blurred and noisy. We augmented with compression, blur, and frequency noise made by perturbing Fourier components. We also used focal loss to concentrate on hard examples:

\[\mathrm{FL}(p_t) = -\alpha (1 - p_t)^\gamma \log(p_t) + 0.6 \cdot \mathrm{BCE}, \quad p_t = e^{-\mathrm{BCE}}\]

We ran a statistical test of how each perturbation changes image features. Frequency noise moved frequency-domain features such as mean frequency; blur moved local binary pattern (LBP) texture features; plain moments like mean, standard deviation, skewness and kurtosis barely changed. The two perturbations hit different parts of the representation, so using both made sense.

Results

Model Accuracy (%) F1
LeViT_192 95.87 0.9586
LeViT_192 + Aug 98.17 0.9817
LeViT_128 + NPR 98.88 0.98
LeViT_192 + NPR + Aug + Frequency Noise 99.21 0.9869

The final combination reached 99.21% on CIFAKE. The lesson was that each piece (representation, augmentation, pretraining at scale) added a bit, and none was sufficient alone.

Explaining the fakes without labels

No dataset provides artifact labels, so we could not train an explainer. Instead, we used the Ovis 1.6 Gemma2-9B vision-language model zero-shot. The input is only images the detector flagged. A single prompt lists the artifacts to look for, such as inconsistent object boundaries, texture bleeding, unrealistic reflections, conflicting light sources and aliasing on high-contrast edges, and asks for a structured reply of artifact names with explanations.

Typical outputs flagged “texture bleeding between adjacent regions”, “artificial noise patterns in uniform surfaces”, blurred airplane edges and distorted window reflections. These are plausible but unverified: there is no ground truth, and some of these artifacts also occur naturally, so false positives are likely.

What did not work or remained open

  • Resolution: at 32x32 subtle artifacts are invisible; high resolution would need much more compute and likely a stronger classifier.
  • Dataset dependence: performance leans on the diversity of the training generators.
  • After the competition, we continued with Adobe Research on out-of-distribution generalisation, looking at adversarial training, jigsaw-style self-supervised learning and continual learning.

For the compact version, see the project page.
entry.summary: LeViT plus Neighboring Pixel Relationships for detection, and a zero-shot VLM for explaining artifacts.

entry.title: Building a Real-Time, Two-Stage Streak Suppressor for Therapy-Guidance Ultrasound

link.title: Building a Real-Time, Two-Stage Streak Suppressor for Therapy-Guidance Ultrasound

entry.content:
When a focused-ultrasound therapy such as HIFU or histotripsy runs, the same time-sensitive question hangs over every treatment: what is happening in the tissue right now? B-mode imaging is the live window, but the therapy field interferes with the imaging field, and the resulting image gets streaks. This post is the story of the work I did with Mihir Agarwal, Ruchika Dhawan, Nishita Mistry and Prof. Himanshu Shekhar at the MUSE Lab (IIT Gandhinagar) between December 2023 and July 2024 to remove them fast enough to be used during therapy.

The constraint: it has to be live

Plenty of ways to clean up an ultrasound image exist if you can afford offline processing. Therapy guidance cannot. If a method is slower than the imaging frame rate, it is useless for the thing it is meant to guide. So from the start the design target was not just “good image quality” but “good quality at a speed no longer a bottleneck”. That one requirement shaped almost every choice below.

The problem has two different halves

Streaks are mostly vertical, bright, thin features that cover some of the image and leave the rest intact. Fixing them involves two different questions:

  1. Where are the streaks? A detection problem, answered by a binary mask.
  2. What should be there instead? An inpainting problem: fill in the masked pixels plausibly from the context.

A single network can try to do both, but each half has a different character. Detection is a segmentation task that U-Nets handle well. Inpainting is about reconstructing missing structure, where frequency-domain information is useful because the streak’s periodic, vertical structure is easy to describe in Fourier space. Keeping the stages separate also means the second network is only asked to fill in masked regions rather than reinterpret the whole image.

First attempt: U-Net plus diffusion

Our first version, presented at the IEEE South Asian Ultrasonics Symposium 2024, paired a U-Net with a diffusion model. The U-Net uses skip connections to find streaks, and the diffusion model, used with text-prompt conditioning, does the inpainting. The initial findings were encouraging: an SNR improvement of 6.0 +/- 3.4 dB, IoU 0.698 for the segmentation, and fast model convergence that hinted at real-time potential. But the abstract itself flags the open questions: validation on diverse datasets and performance optimization were future work.

An iterative sampling process is intrinsically heavier than one forward pass, so for a >440 FPS target a feed-forward restoration network is the natural direction.

The two-stage pipeline

The version in the repository, Fourier-StreakNet, has these parts:

  • Streak segmentation. A multi-channel U-Net (the repository also has a variant using a frequency-domain notch filter) outputs a streak mask.
  • Restoration. A U-Net with Fourier attention layers inpaints the masked regions. The attention operates on frequency-domain features, which is where streak structure is concentrated.
  • Evaluation. The toolkit reports IoU and Dice for the mask, and PSNR and signal-to-interference ratio (SIR) for the restored images.

On the CV-reported measurements, the full pipeline runs at over 440 FPS and improves reconstruction by 13.7 dB.

The data problem and the synthetic-streak fix

The biggest practical obstacle was data. You rarely have a perfectly clean twin of an image that was streaked. Our fix was to manufacture the pairs. We isolated images that had no streaks, augmented them to increase the dataset size, and then added random streaks using heuristic functions. Because we create the streaks, we know exactly where they are, so the exact mask for training the segmentation U-Net comes for free, and the clean original is the restoration target. We then split the result into training and validation sets.

The streak intensity profile mattered. Real streaks are not uniform bars, so we modulated their intensity with Gaussian profiles, and generated data across several ultrasound domains to encourage robust generalization instead of overfitting to a single imaging setup.

Honest caveats

  • Numbers vary by stage of the work. The SAUS abstract reports 6.0 +/- 3.4 dB for the early U-Net plus diffusion system, while the later two-stage pipeline is reported at +13.7 dB. These are different systems and should not be compared directly.
  • Synthetic is not real. A model trained on synthetic streaks can only be as good as the synthetic generator. The gap to real interference patterns is the main risk, which is why the abstract’s “validate on diverse datasets” remains the key next step.
  • Speed is for the pipeline as measured, not a clinical guarantee. Integrating with a live therapy system is another engineering step.

Lessons

  1. Decompose by what each part is good at. Detection and inpainting are different problems; separating them let each network stay small and fast.
  2. Let the speed requirement drive architecture early. Iterative sampling is inherently heavier than a single forward pass, which matters when the target is real time.
  3. When you lack paired data, build the generator carefully. The quality of your synthetic degradation model is the ceiling on what the restoration network learns.
  4. Report numbers with their context. Three systems, three sets of metrics; tie each to a source.

Links

  • Project page: Streak artifact suppression
  • Code: agarwal-mihir/Fourier-StreakNet
  • Poster: SAUS 2024
entry.summary: Why we split streak removal into segmentation plus Fourier-attention inpainting, and how that got us past 440 FPS.

entry.title: Teaching Machine Learning Through Interactive Apps

link.title: Teaching Machine Learning Through Interactive Apps

entry.content:
Equations are a poor first contact with an algorithm. You can stare at the Adam update for an hour and still not know what changing \(\beta_2\) does to the path of a ball rolling down a loss surface. In a CS299 project advised by Prof. Nipun Batra, Vannsh Jani, Viraj Vekaria and I (with Kishan Ved on several topics) tried a different route: for each concept, write a blog post with from-scratch code, and build a small app so the reader can poke at it. This post collects what we built, what broke, and what we would do again. The project page is here.

The recipe

Each topic followed the same loop:

  1. Learn the concept well enough to implement it with NumPy only.
  2. Write a Quarto blog post: motivation, maths, code, static plots.
  3. Decide what the reader should be able to change, and expose exactly that in a Streamlit app.
  4. Check the app against a trusted implementation.

Step 3 is the interesting one. A good app has two or three controls, not twelve. For the optimizer demo the controls are the optimizer, the learning rate, momentum and the starting point. Everything else is fixed so that the effect of each knob is legible.

Optimizers: first lessons in being slow

Our first optimizer app redrew the loss curve after every epoch so the path would animate. It was unusable: plotting dominated the runtime and, worse, you only saw the final state because the screen refreshed too late. The fix was boring. Store the iterates in a list, plot once at the end, and give up the live animation. Later, a “Next Step” button on a contour plot restored the sense of motion by letting the reader advance the optimizer one step at a time:

\[\theta_{t+1} = \theta_t - \alpha\,\hat m_t / (\sqrt{\hat v_t}+\epsilon)\]

Seeing momentum overshoot a narrow valley and swing back teaches more than the paragraph describing it. We also added a one-dimensional function with a saddle, a local minimum and a global minimum, with a slider over learning rates that plays a video of Adam’s path. Small learning rates get stuck; large ones skip the basin.

As a sanity check we contributed from-scratch optimizers to the open-source wimpyML library and compared them against PyTorch. On MNIST, our RMSProp reached 97.11% test accuracy versus 97.31% for torch.optim.RMSprop, with nearly the same training time (about 115.7 s versus 113.3 s for 10 iterations). Matching a reference implementation is what lets you trust an explanatory app.

Information theory: watching a tree grow

For Huffman coding, Kishan and I wrote the blog around a min-heap: repeatedly pop the two least frequent symbols, merge them, push the parent back. The app shows both the heap and the tree at each step, so a reader sees why frequent symbols end up near the root. The same machinery reappears in JPEG, where the quantized DCT coefficients are turned into (run, size) pairs and then Huffman-coded; a second app shows that encoding and decoding, and a Colab notebook walks through the whole pipeline: RGB to YCbCr, chroma subsampling, DCT, quantization, entropy coding.

Vannsh took on the neighbouring topics: Shannon-Fano coding, noisy channel coding (with plots of bit error probability against message length and rate), mutual information, and SIREN, which stores an audio clip or an image as the weights of a small network with sinusoidal activations. SIRENs reconstruct beautifully and compress well, but the report is honest about the catch: training on one image takes on the order of an hour, so it is not practical without further optimization.

Fisher information, Jacobians and CORDIC

My own topics were the ones where a picture changes the intuition most.

Fisher information measures how sensitive the likelihood is to a parameter \(\theta\): high information means the data pins \(\theta\) down tightly. The app lets you choose a distribution (normal, Poisson, binomial) and parameters and shows the resulting information.

Change of variables is the Jacobian determinant in

\[\iiint f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz = \iiint f(u,v,w)\,|\det J|\,du\,dv\,dw .\]
The app takes a transformation and shows how a small patch of space is stretched, which makes $$ \det J $$ feel like what it is: a local area (or volume) scale factor.

CORDIC, built with Viraj, rotates a vector toward a target angle by a sequence of shifts and adds, using no multiplications. The app draws the start vector, the current vector, a reference circle and the running sine and cosine; each press of “Next Iteration” applies one more rotation, and you can watch the red arrow close in on the blue one.

What failed, and lessons

  • Too much interactivity. Our design rule became two or three controls per app; every extra knob makes the effect of each one harder to see.
  • Speed is a feature. Our per-epoch redraw showed that slow interaction kills exploration. Precompute, cache, and plot once.
  • The blog comes first. In our view the apps work best with a written explanation that told the reader what to look for. An app without a question to answer is a toy.
  • Validate against a reference. Autodiff, optimizers and Huffman codes were all checked against PyTorch or a library before we put them in front of readers.
  • Learning is the real output. As the report notes, a lot of the early work on each task went into learning the concept before any visualization was possible.

Links

  • Project page: Visualizations for Machine Learning
  • Full write-up: project notion page
  • Apps: Fisher information, Huffman, JPEG coding, CORDIC, change of variables, velocity viz, noisy channel coding

Thanks to Prof. Nipun Batra for the opportunity to learn machine learning this way.
entry.summary: What we learned building blogs and Streamlit apps for Huffman coding, CORDIC, Fisher information and optimizers.
